extraction.document_type: NBER working paper; narrative review essay (not peer reviewed)

extraction.research_question: What empirical facts about lobbying are broadly agreed, what challenges block causal inference on lobbying effects, which quasi-experimental and structural methods can overcome them, and which data sources and open questions should drive the next generation of research (essay has no original estimates).
extraction.theory: Informational lobbying: lobbying is the transfer of information in private meetings between interest groups and politicians; politicians maximize re-election, promotion and ideological goals (p.4). Hannan-Freeman-Carroll population ecology (legitimation and competition) for counts of interest groups (pp.8-9). Expertise versus connections (who you know vs what you know) (pp.9-10). Counteractive lobbying (Austen-Smith and Wright) versus legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff) for targeting (p.11). Calls for empirical testing of formal models (EITM) (p.40).
extraction.data: No sample of its own. Cited studies: Blanes i Vidal et al (2012) former congressional staffers who are contract lobbyists, 22 periods (pp.18-19); de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006) university earmarks 1997-1999 (pp.22-24); Richter et al (2009) public firms, tax rates, about 10 percent lobby (pp.24-26); de Figueiredo and Cameron (2012) 38 US states (p.8); Baumgartner et al (2009) 98 issues, 2,200 advocates (p.13); Kang (2012) energy groups (p.27); Jayachandran (2006) stock returns, 2001 Jeffords switch (pp.20-21).
extraction.method: Narrative review and methods primer. Surveys the empirical facts on who lobbies, how much, and how it is organized (Sec II), then reviews five designs: difference-in-differences with exogenous shocks, event studies, instrumental variables (2SLS), two-step Heckman selection models, and structural modeling (Sec III.B). Also lists matching, regression discontinuity and synthetic control as untried for lobbying (p.29). Compares data classes: surveys, registries, transaction reports (Sec IV).
extraction.identification: Difference-in-differences: politician exits (retirement or defeat) as exogenous shock to lobbyist revenue, with lobbyist and party-chamber-time fixed effects. Event study: Jeffords party switch as shock to firm abnormal returns. IV: university overhead rates as cost shifter instrument for lobbying, excluded from earmark equation. Selection: probit selection equation with liquid assets as excluded variable, inverse Mills ratio added to tax equation. Structural: all-pay contest model estimated on policy votes.
extraction.measures: Lobbying expenditures from federal LDA and state transaction reports; counts of registered groups and lobbyists; lobbyist revenue; effective tax rates; earmark dollars; abnormal stock returns; soft money as party alignment; overhead rates as instrument; liquid assets as selection variable; inverse Mills ratio.
extraction.scope: Mostly US federal and state lobbying (LDA federal data, US state transaction data), with brief mention of Japan, China, India, Mexico, Norway and other developed or transition economies (p.35-36). Literature reviewed through 2013; federal disclosure under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 (p.34). Excludes campaign finance, illegal lobbying and bribery, and bureaucratic lobbying (footnote 1, p.4).
key_findings: Federal lobbying spending was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, against roughly 750 million a year in interest-group campaign contributions, about five times as large (Sec II.A, pp.5-6).
Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of federal lobbying expenditures; issue-ideology membership groups about 2 percent (de Figueiredo 2004 as cited, Sec II.A, p.6).

Only about 10 percent of publicly traded firms lobby on their own behalf (Richter et al 2009; Kerr et al 2013); a firm lobbying last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability (Sec II.A, p.7).
Budgeting periods are associated with a 19 percent increase in state interest-group lobbying expenditures across 38 states (de Figueiredo 2014; de Figueiredo and Cameron 2012) (Sec II.A, p.8).

Lobbyist revenue falls about 23 percent after the senator they formerly served is defeated or retires (Blanes i Vidal et al 2012) (Sec II.C, p.10); the essay attributes about 23 percent of lobbying services value to who you know (Sec III.B.1, p.20).

Richter et al (2009): a 1 percent increase in lobbying over baseline predicts a 1.07 percentage point lower effective tax rate in the next period, and the result survives a Heckman selection correction (Sec III.B.4, p.26).
de Figueiredo and Silverman (2006): lobbying raises earmarks only when the district legislator sits on an appropriations committee; no significant effect otherwise (Sec III.B.3, p.24).
Kang (2012) structural all-pay contest: expenditure effects on enactment are very small, but the marginal return in policy is about 140 percent (Sec III.B.5, p.28).
Jayachandran (2006): firms more aligned with the former Republican majority lost market value after the Jeffords switch (Sec III.B.2, p.21).
Baumgartner et al (2009): across 98 issues, both sides mobilize roughly equal resources; policies are stable and change, when it occurs, is substantial (Sec II.D, p.13).
Targeting: powerful, allied and marginal legislators are lobbied; staunch enemies are not. Counteractive and subsidy accounts give different predictions (Sec II.C, pp.10-11).
State interest-group counts follow an inverted-U over time from legitimation then competition, and rise with economy size and number of issues (Sec II.B, pp.8-9).
limitations: Essay itself reports no new estimates; its consensus claims are a synthesis of cited work (p.2-3, Sec II).
Lobbying panels show persistence and little within-group variation, so fixed effects need external shocks (Sec III.A, p.16).
Omitted variables are pervasive because some instruments of influence are unobserved (p.16-17).
Endogenous selection into lobbying is not random; about 10 percent of interests lobby, so returns may be biased upward (p.17).

Difference-in-differences can have inconsistent standard errors; event windows can be confounded; weak instruments and small selection samples can doom IV and selection models; structural assumptions may be unbelievable (footnote 3, p.28).
Survey data suffers from non-response, non-random samples, recall error and little verifiability (p.32).
Registries count groups, include zero-spend registrants, and mix rules across jurisdictions (p.33).
Transaction data gives spending and intensity but not message content and not which legislator was targeted (pp.34-35).
Outcome variables are often weakly linked to lobbying; authors call for institutional detail on the link (p.30).

summary_md: De Figueiredo and Richter (NBER WP 19698, 2013) is a narrative review with no new estimates. It sets out what the field agreed on about lobbying by 2013 and how to study it causally. The scale facts: federal lobbying was about 3.5 billion dollars in 2012, roughly five times interest-group campaign contributions. Corporations and trade associations account for over 84 percent of it. Only about 10 percent of public firms lobby, and a firm that lobbied last year lobbies this year with 92 percent probability. Its main argument is that lobbying panels are persistent, selected and confounded by unobserved channels. Fixed effects alone therefore cannot identify effects, and research should use exogenous shocks. The designs it reviews are difference-in-differences on legislator exits, event studies such as the Jeffords switch, cost-shifter instruments, Heckman selection, and structural all-pay contest models. It cites conditional returns: earmark gains only where the home legislator sits on Appropriations, a 1.07 percentage point lower tax rate per 1 percent more lobbying, and about 23 percent of lobbyist revenue lost when a former boss leaves office. It also notes that transaction (LDA) data record spending but not which legislator was targeted. For Paul's systems the essay mostly confirms choices already made. It agrees that the lobbied-member link is circular (LD-2 names no member) and explains why the sector-growth lobbying coefficient flips under year fixed effects. It also shows that the influence engine's money legs cover only PAC contributions, the smaller channel. Its shock-based designs point to tests the system has not run. Nothing in it argues for either rejected SNA proposal. Its revolving-door evidence must not be turned into influence language on staffer edges.

summary_issues: Says the essay agrees the lobbied-member link is circular. The essay never argues or uses that idea; it only says disclosure rules do not require identifying targeted legislators (pp.11, 34-35). Circularity is the system's own finding in the brain.

Says the essay explains why the sector-growth lobbying coefficient flips under year fixed effects. The essay does not discuss that regression; it only says persistent panels need external shocks (pp.16-17).
Says the essay shows the influence engine's money legs cover only PAC contributions. The essay says nothing about the engine; that is a fact about the code, not an essay finding.
Says fixed effects alone cannot identify effects. The essay says they need exogenous shocks, a softer claim than cannot identify.
Says lobbyist revenue is lost when a former boss leaves office. The essay's design uses defeat or retirement of the senator served (pp.10, 18-19).
Says selection makes return estimates biased upward without condition. The essay conditions this on non-lobbying interests expecting no return (p.17).
Says the 1.07 point tax effect is per 1 percent more lobbying. The essay says per 1 percent over the firm's baseline, predicted in the next period (p.26).
Says the essay mostly confirms choices already made in Paul's systems. That is an analyst judgment beyond the text, not an essay finding.
gaps_exposed: The influence engine's money legs (flip model and money response) model only PAC contributions, the smaller of the two money channels; the system states no explicit position on how sector lobbying, about five times larger, relates to member winnability.

No lobbying-return number used anywhere in the system is identified by the shock-based designs the essay recommends (member exits, party switches, cost shifters). Break-even and ROI floors rest on an assumed saturating form.
Selection into lobbying (about 10 percent of firms) is not modeled in the sector-growth lobbying regressions. Sector sums over registrants mix the extensive and intensive margins.

Legislator exits (retirement or defeat) are an available exogenous shock in the staffer and member data and could support a difference-in-differences test of route or engagement value. This has not been designed.
The break-even and ROI component's recorded code_ref (fec/templates/make_dashboard_html_00.tpl) does not exist at that path in the live tree, so the component card is stale.
flags: Revolving-door evidence (23 percent revenue loss) is phrased in the paper as the value of who you know; it must not become influence or access language on staffer or revolving-door edges (brain rule; D-025).

Cited return estimates (Richter et al 1.07 percentage points per 1 percent lobbying; Kang 140 percent policy return) are pooled over firms and sectors. Quote them only with an UNSTRATIFIED label, and do not use them as dollar-ROI calibration.

The essay's call to link transaction data to targeted legislators would, if done through LDA bill rosters, recreate the circular lobbied-member link and conflict with D-021 (LDA is an identity source, not an edge or weight source).
The essay does not argue for dropping regular cosponsorship edges or for per-edge volume normalization; no rejected SNA proposal is involved.
The essay is a 2013 working paper, not peer reviewed, and reports no original estimates; every number is a secondary citation.
paul_alignment: Paul left no annotation on this work (0 notes). By component, Paul frames lobbying as ROI, expects donations to lead lobbying, and read Kim and Kunisky as a way to identify champion members. The essay agrees with the system rather than with those notes on three points. Naive lobbying returns are biased upward by selection and persistence. Contributions and lobbying are distinct channels of very different scale, which fits the near-zero bridge partial. Disclosure data cannot say which legislator was lobbied, which fits the circular-link ruling. His ROI enthusiasm and his expectation of a donation lead are therefore stale relative to the system now. His wish for explicit inter-industry conflict on bills is supported by the contest-model literature the essay reviews.

extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (72,168 chars, 1,309 lines): front matter, abstract, introduction, conceptual framework, data, all results sections (4.1-4.3), conclusion, references, Tables 1-6, Figures 1-3 (text labels only; page images not rendered), and Appendix A (dataset construction, matching) and B (Table 7, RD placebo figures 4-6). Metadata hint corrected: co-author is Brian Kelleher Richter. Annotations: p.annot_sha12s is empty and no _annots file matches sha12 0dc33fec3429, so paul_markup is empty (0 items; 0 dropped). p.note is not set, so this is not one of Paul's own notes. Topic coverage: lobbying yes; allocation yes; elections yes; legislators only indirectly (candidate-level giving); networks no; path-finding no; persuasion or turnout no; text measurement no. Table 3 column alignment is ambiguous in the text extraction; column numbers follow the paper's own prose.
extraction.research_question: Do statutory limits on corporate PAC campaign contributions generate spillover increases in other corporate political activity, namely CEO contributions to the same candidates and firm lobbying expenditures, at the regulated per-candidate contribution threshold?
extraction.theory: Revealed-preference firm model (Section 2, pp.5-7): firms give to candidates until marginal benefit equals the dollar; a binding per-candidate cap creates a positive shadow price, so firms substitute toward other channels. Lobbying is also read as a legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006) and as a possible cost of access. The authors state the design is theory-agnostic and is not a test of theories of firm political behavior (p.4).
extraction.data: S&P 500 firms present at any point 1991-2008; 950 firms in contribution data. Contributions: FEC filings via Center for Responsive Politics bulk data; CEO identity and firm characteristics from COMPUSTAT/ExecuComp; PAC-to-firm mapping from Myers (2005). Unit for PAC and CEO models: firm-candidate-cycle, 6,803,661 observations over nine federal cycles, 1992-2008. Lobbying: LDA disclosures for engagements over 10,000 dollars, 2000-2008, firm-cycle unit; 2,796 firm-cycle observations stated in Section 3 (p.8); regression samples 2,783 observations and 787 firms (Table 3, p.29), 1,908 observations and 579 lobbying firms (Table 3 columns 4-6), 4,821 observations and 943 firms (placebos, Table 4), 2,200 or 2,191 observations and 700 or 693 firms (RD, Table 5).
extraction.method: Linear probability and OLS. CEO model (eq. 3, p.10): binary CEO-to-candidate contribution on PAC contributed and PAC at-limit indicators with firm-by-cycle and candidate-by-cycle fixed effects. Lobbying model (eq. 4, p.13): firm-cycle aggregate lobbying on PAC contributed and at-limit indicators with firm fixed effects and Fama-French 49 industry-by-cycle fixed effects. One-sided regression discontinuity (eq. 5, p.16): polynomial (linear or quadratic) in PAC dollars with a jump at the limit, with and without industry-cycle fixed effects. Difference-in-differences around BCRA (post-2003 cycle indicator, Table 6, p.18). Standard errors clustered by firm. Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) selection-on-unobservables ratio reported for the main lobbying model (p.14).
extraction.identification: CEO model: within firm-cycle, cross-candidate variation across the statutory per-candidate limit, assuming firm-by-candidate-by-cycle factors are orthogonal to CEO giving (p.4). Lobbying model: firm and industry-cycle fixed effects, plus assumed smoothness of lobbying absent regulation, which the authors test on advertising, R&D and dividends in the appendix (p.4-5, p.A-4 to A-7). RD: assumes optimization frictions so firms cannot perfectly control PAC dollars around the limit; authors call this strong (p.17). BCRA 2002 soft-money ban is the only exogenous policy change; it leaves PAC limits intact. The authors say there is no exogenous variation in FEC limits, so results are partial correlations (p.14).
extraction.scope: US federal elections; large publicly traded S&P 500 firms with PACs; contributions 1992-2008; lobbying 2000-2008, so only a single pre-BCRA lobbying cycle. Excludes state politics, super PACs (post-window), independent expenditures and in-kind or philanthropic channels (pp.19-20).
key_findings: CEO supplementary giving (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC raises the probability a CEO gives to that candidate by 0.066 (SE 0.006). The text instead reports 7.7 percent (Section 4.1, p.11), a mismatch noted here.

CEO dollars (Table 2, p.28): at-limit PAC associated with 109.92 extra dollars (SE 10.05). Text reports 123 dollars (p.11); Table 7 (p.A-4) gives 123.88 (SE 10.55). Figure 2 shows 59.91 for the 4,500-4,999 bin versus the at-limit value.

Lobbying main estimate (Table 3 column 1, p.29; text p.14): firms whose PAC reaches the limit for any candidate spend 549,166 dollars more per cycle (SE 225,013; significant at 1 percent). Abstract gives a range of 549,000 to 1.6M dollars.
Lobbying firms only (Table 3 column 6, p.29; text p.15): at-limit coefficient 662,590 dollars (SE 305,066; significant at 5 percent).

Large-expenditure control (Table 3 columns 2-3, p.14-15): PAC-large-expenditure indicator is not significant; at-limit remains significant when both are included, about 250,000 dollars larger than the large-expenditure coefficient per text. Altonji-Elder-Taber ratio stated as 7.7 (p.14).

Placebo outcomes (Table 4, p.30; text p.15): at-limit coefficients are R&D 63.07 (SE 68.56), advertising 4.71 (SE 34.74), dividends -23.02 (SE 66.93), acquisitions 5.32 (SE 103.31); none significant. Units not stated in the paper.

One-sided RD on lobbying (Table 5, p.30; text pp.16-17): jump of 3,001,984 (linear, no industry-cycle FE), 2,427,612 (quadratic), 2,250,564 (linear, industry-cycle FE) and 1,630,744 (quadratic, industry-cycle FE), all significant at 1 percent. Figure 3 (p.26) plots the discontinuity.

summary_md: Fremeth, Richter and Schaufele (MPRA working paper, 2018) ask whether the federal per-candidate cap on corporate PAC gifts (5,000 dollars per election, 10,000 per cycle) pushes firms into other political channels. They use S&P 500 firms with PACs, 1992-2008 FEC data (6.8M firm-candidate-cycle rows) and LDA lobbying for 2000-2008 (about 2,800 firm-cycles). Within a firm-cycle, a candidate who receives the PAC maximum is 6.6 points more likely to also receive a gift from the firm's CEO (Table 2), about 110 dollars more on average. Firms whose PAC maxes out any candidate spend about 549,000 dollars more on lobbying per cycle, with firm and industry-by-cycle fixed effects. A one-sided regression discontinuity at the limit gives jumps of 1.6M to 3.0M dollars, but the authors call its frictions assumption strong. Placebo outcomes (R&D, advertising, dividends, acquisitions) show no jump. The authors say no exogenous variation in the limit exists, so the estimates are partial correlations. Some numbers in the text do not match the tables. For Paul's systems, the paper bears mainly on how money is bounded. The Melange optimizer treats the 10,000-dollar PAC limit as the ceiling on CU spend per member, and the flip model counts competitor money only as bank and finserv PAC dollars. The paper suggests firms at the cap shift resources into executive giving and lobbying, which neither ledger sees. Mentat already tiers Chief-level employee giving by company, so a PAC-at-limit by Chief-giving join is a cheap extension. The paper's firm-level link between giving and lobbying does not contradict the member-level FEC-LDA bridge null. That bridge asks a different question, and the paper itself notes that LDA filings name no candidates.

extraction.research_question: Why does bipartisanship persist in Congress despite polarization and primary threats? The paper asks whether legislators who attract a larger share of opposite-party cosponsors on their bills are more effective at advancing them, whether that holds across eras and party conditions, whether the effect has an optimum, and whether offering bipartisan cosponsorships in turn drives attracting them (reciprocity).
extraction.data: Sample: all Representatives and Senators serving in the 93rd-114th Congresses (1973-2016); independents excluded. Unit: legislator by two-year Congress. Bills: all public bills introduced in the period. Cosponsorship data for 93rd-110th Congresses from Fowler (2006), updated by the authors for 111th-114th. N: House 8,997 to 9,202 legislator-Congress observations; Senate 2,167 to 2,192 (Table 1). Hitchhiker law sample (Table A11): 4,494 House observations, 1993-2014.
extraction.method: Cross-sectional time-series least squares regressions with legislator fixed effects and robust standard errors (Tables 1-3, A2-A13); pooled OLS and fixed-effects OLS for reciprocity regressions (Table 4, clustered SEs in pooled models). Nonlinear models add a squared term. Robustness: commemorative-bill exclusion, normalization by Congress, cosponsorship-level controls, low-cosponsorship eras, binary alternative measures, Lugar index, no member FE, electoral safety interactions, later legislative stages, hitchhiker-inclusive law counts, and era splits (pre/post 1994).
extraction.scope: US Congress, House and Senate, 1973-2016, public bills only. Population is all members in that window. The argument concerns individual lawmaking effectiveness, not chamber-level outcomes; the 60-vote cloture environment is offered to explain higher Senate levels.
key_findings: Table 1 Model 1.2 (House, p.17): proportion bipartisan cosponsors attracted = 0.433 (SE 0.097), p<0.001; Model 1.5 (Senate, p.17) = 0.330 (SE 0.147), p<0.05. One SD increase = +0.08 LES in House and +0.06 in Senate, about 6-8 percent of mean LES of 1.0 (p.16).

Uncontrolled Models 1.1 (House 0.986) and 1.4 (Senate 0.538) are larger; the coefficient on proportion bipartisan cosponsorships offered is not significant with controls (Model 1.3 = -0.234; Model 1.6 = -0.420) (p.17-18).
Robust to excluding commemorative bills, normalizing by Congress, controlling for cosponsorship levels, binary alternative measures (Table A5 House 0.213, p<0.001) and the Lugar index (p.18-19).
Without member fixed effects coefficients are larger (Table A6 with controls: House 0.552, p<0.001; Senate 0.440, p<0.001) (p.18-19, Appendix p.10).

Table 2 (p.20-21): effect stays positive and significant (House 0.432 to 0.629; Senate 0.358 to 0.442) when interacted with a Congress counter, majority margin or party polarization; all interactions small and not significant.

Table 3 nonlinearity (p.22-23): House linear 1.828 and squared -1.844 peak at 0.496; Senate 1.666 and -1.626 peak at 0.512. A one-SD decline costs about 22 percent of LES in House and 16 percent in Senate; a one-SD rise adds about 8 and 4 percent (p.24).

Majority and minority subsamples show similar nonlinear shapes (Table 3 Models 3.2-3.3, 3.5-3.6). Authors read the larger majority coefficients as a scale artifact, since majority LES is about three times minority LES (p.24-25).
Reciprocity (Table 4, p.27): offering bipartisan cosponsorships predicts attracting them. House pooled 0.626 (SE 0.039); House with member FE 0.317; Senate pooled 0.739; Senate FE 0.547; all p<0.001.
Distance from median predicts fewer bipartisan cosponsors in pooled models (House -0.154, Senate -0.114) but the House effect disappears with member FE (0.005) (p.27).

Later stages (Table A8, House, Appendix p.12): bipartisan share predicts action in committee 0.894, beyond committee 0.853, passing chamber 0.800, and becoming law 0.485 (all p<0.001). Senate committee-stage model A9.2 is not significant (1.767); Senate law model A9.5 = 0.589 (p<0.05) (Appendix p.13).

extraction.theory: Two competing hypotheses. Bipartisanship and Effectiveness: spatial models (Krehbiel 1998) imply successful bills need pivotal veto-player support; bipartisan support signals quality to gatekeepers (Koger 2003) and refines proposals (p.4-6). Partisanship and Effectiveness: leaders reward one-sided party support (Cox and McCubbins 2005; Hastert Rule), and policy specialists achieve more (Bernhard and Sulkin 2018) (p.6-7). Conditional hypotheses cover majority status, era and polarization (p.7-8). Reciprocity: offering cross-party cosponsorships generates reciprocal ones (p.25-26).
extraction.identification: No instrument, natural experiment or design-based strategy. Identification relies on legislator fixed effects (within-member variation), a standard covariate set from the effectiveness literature, and robustness checks. Authors interpret coefficients as associations and separately test the offered-vs-attracted distinction (p.15-18). Reverse causation and time-varying confounds are not formally addressed.

summary_md: Harbridge-Yong, Volden and Wiseman ask whether bipartisanship pays for individual lawmakers. They use all House and Senate members in the 93rd-114th Congresses (1973-2016; about 9,000 House and 2,170 Senate legislator-Congress rows) and regress the Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score on the share of a member's cosponsors who come from the other party. The design uses legislator fixed effects. That attracted share predicts effectiveness: within member, the coefficient is 0.433 in the House and 0.330 in the Senate, so one SD is worth about 6-8 percent of mean LES. The share members offer to the other party's bills does not predict effectiveness once controls are in. The effect holds across eras, majority margins and polarization levels, and in majority and minority strata. It is an inverted U that peaks near a 50/50 cosponsor mix (0.496 House, 0.512 Senate). In the House the attracted share also predicts each later stage, from committee action to law. Offering cross-party cosponsorships predicts attracting them, at 0.317 within member in the House and 0.547 in the Senate. The evidence is observational, with one-tailed tests and no design-based identification. For Paul's system, the sharpest point concerns direction. bpf is an undirected, symmetrized cross-party tie share. Cooperation v2's directional component measures offered support. Nothing in the system measures attracted support, which is the side the paper ties to effectiveness. The flip model's (1+0.3 bpf) passage bonus and the coalition seed boost (1+0.8 bpf) are monotone, but the paper finds a peak and then a decline. The paper's reciprocity is cosponsorship exchange. It does not validate the money reciprocity in D-104..D-108. Any transfer is UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced on Paul's data.

extraction.title: No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
extraction.document_type: working paper (manuscript with supplementary materials S1-S48); no journal or venue named in text
extraction.coverage: Read all 4038 lines of the text in six chunks: front matter, abstract, intro, theory, data, method, results, threats, conclusion, references, and supplementary S2-S48. Figures read as axis labels only. Annotations: annot_sha12s empty, no _annots file, so paul_markup is empty (0 items, 0 dropped); not a Paul note. Corrections: year 2022 changed to 2021 (text: This version October 08, 2021); venue cleared (only UCL affiliations in text). Title and authors confirmed.
extraction.research_question: Have gender gaps in parliamentary debating style, measured against gender stereotypes, narrowed in the UK House of Commons since 1997, and are women moving toward agentic styles over time (p.2-3, p.12)?
extraction.theory: Gender role and role congruity theory (Eagly and Karau 2002): stereotypes produce conformity through internalised standards and social sanctions. Stereotypes are dynamic (Diekman and Eagly 2000): changing social roles, public attitudes and women's rising parliamentary presence should weaken conformity pressure (p.9-13). Rival feminist institutionalism predicts women move toward communal styles as their numbers and power grow (p.13, p.26-28). The authors do not separate the mechanisms (p.12, p.29).
extraction.data: UK House of Commons debate speeches, May 1997 to March 2019 (source not named in text). Unit: one MP's speech-document per debate. Sample: 14,864 debates, 1,422 MPs (370 female, 1,052 male), 418,147 MP-debate observations (p.14-15); nearly half a million speeches (p.4). 20 parliamentary sessions, about 635 MPs per session, each MP in about 9 sessions on average (p.20). Speeches under 50 words, the Speaker's contributions and debates with fewer than five participants are dropped (p.15).
extraction.method: Eight style measures from text. Six use word-embedding expanded seed dictionaries (GloVe, 150 dimensions, window 3; sigmoid rescaling a=40, c=0.35; TF-IDF weighted sentence scores) (p.15-17, S2-S7). Complexity uses rescaled Flesch-Kincaid. Repetition uses Lempel-Ziv compression ratio. Measures standardised to mean 0, SD 1. Outcome model: Bayesian dynamic hierarchical normal model in Stan, one fit per style (three chains, 500 iterations after 250 burn-in); MP-by-session intercepts, debate random effects, random-walk priors on male baseline and female gap across sessions (p.19-22).
extraction.identification: Observational design, no causal identification strategy. Gender gaps are identified from within-debate variation because debate random effects absorb topic and debate differences (p.22-23). Robustness checks: covariate model (S20-S24), debate-type models (S25-S29), within-MP versus replacement decomposition (S30-S35), topic confounding with correlated topic models K=10 to 80 (S36-S43), and a participation test (S44-S46).
extraction.scope: UK House of Commons floor debate, 1997-2019. Population is MPs who speak in debates with five or more participants. Not campaign speech, votes, or voter sanctions. Covers the post-1997 era through 2019, with women rising from 18% to 32% of seats (p.11-12).
extraction.measures: Eight styles (Table 1, p.9). Communal: human narrative, affect, positive emotion. Agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression, negative emotion. Human validation of text scores against coder judgements (two coders, about 70 comparisons per style): correlations about 0.61 to 0.85 (Table S4, p.S17). Dictionary benchmark correlations are lower, e.g. positive emotion 0.38 and 0.34 against 0.70 and 0.71 for the embedding measure (p.S19).
key_findings: Early period: female MPs use more human narrative, affect and positive emotion, while men use more aggression and complexity, at least before 2010 (p.23-24).
Fact, repetition and negative emotion run against stereotype: women use them more than men for much of the period (p.23-24).
Six of eight styles: MP gender explains less between-MP variation in style at the end of the period than at the start (p.4).
For styles that converge, the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls by between 29% and 60% comparing periods before and after 2007 (p.25).
Fact and negative emotion diverge: gender explains about 0.6% and 2% of variation in 1997-2007, rising to about 4% and 9% after 2007 (p.25).
Aggression, complexity, affect and positive emotion gaps shrink to no consistent difference in recent years; the repetition gap stays relatively stable (p.23-26).
Change is concentrated among women: their communal styles decline while their negative emotion, fact and aggression rise, and men stay relatively stable on those (p.26-27).
Within-MP versus replacement: neither mechanism alone explains the convergence; divergence in negative emotion is almost entirely differential replacement of MPs (p.28; S30-S35).
Validation: text measures outperform standard dictionaries against human codings for every style except fact (p.S17-S19).
Covariate model (party, government status, frontbench, committee chair, age, margin, degree, occupation) leaves the main trends intact; aggression and complexity attenuate (p.28; S21-S22).
Topic confounding: a style gap on a topic largely does not predict that topic's growth; results hold for 10 to 80 topics (p.28; S40-S43).
Participation: an MP's average style does not predict how many speeches they make, so selection into debate does not drive the trends (p.28-29; S44-S45).
limitations: Voter sanctions for counter-stereotypic behaviour are not measured, so the mechanism linking debate style to voter penalties is untested (p.29-30).
Mechanisms are not separated: the authors do not disentangle the three pathways they outline (p.12, p.29).
Only legislative debate is studied; campaign communication, where voter penalties may bite harder, is not examined (p.31).
Seed dictionaries for aggression and human narrative were built by the authors from close reading (p.15).
Repetition is validated only at sentence level, which the authors concede is less suited to that concept (S18 note 3).
Complexity gap shift between 2008 and 2013 is confounded by covariates, and aggression and complexity trends attenuate (p.28; S21-S22).
Flesch-Kincaid chosen over domain-specific complexity measures for simplicity (p.17-18).
Sampler run is short (three chains, 500 iterations after 250 burn-in) (p.22).
Number of topics K is not fixed a priori; results rely on the sweep 10 to 80 (S41).

summary_md: Hargrave and Blumenau (UCL working paper; the text is dated October 2021, filed here as 2022) track how gendered debating style changed in the UK House of Commons between May 1997 and March 2019. The corpus is 418,147 MP-debate observations: 1,422 MPs across 14,864 debates. They score eight styles. Three are communal: human narrative, affect and positive emotion. Five are agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression and negative emotion. Six of the measures come from seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe embeddings, and these beat standard dictionaries against human coding for every style except fact (positive emotion about 0.70 against 0.38). Each style goes through a Bayesian dynamic hierarchical model with debate random effects, so gender gaps are estimated within debates. Early in the period, women used more communal styles and men more aggression and complexity. Women also used more fact, repetition and negative emotion, which runs against the stereotype. For six of eight styles the share of between-MP variation explained by gender fell, by 29 to 60 percent comparing the periods before and after 2007. Fact and negative emotion went the other way, rising to about 4 and 9 percent of MP-level variation after 2007. The change sits mostly with women, whose communal styles declined. The work is observational and does not separate mechanisms. For Paul's systems, the main point is that agency, communion and negative-emotion text scores can carry a gender signature that changes over time. The persona channel and affective N in the receptivity layer check for a party signature but not for gender. This is UK floor debate measured with dictionaries, not the US Congress, so any transfer is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

bearings.paper_claim: Communal styles (human narrative, affect, positive emotion) were higher among female MPs early in the period. Positive emotion and affect show no consistent significant gender gap by the latest years; the human narrative gap narrows gradually but is not stated to reach zero. For six of eight styles gender explains less between-MP style variation at the end of the period than at the start. For the converging styles the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls 29 to 60 percent comparing pre-2007 with post-2007; the converging styles are not named individually. Window: UK Commons May 1997 to March 2019. Denominator: MP-by-session variation (R2-style metric).

extraction.title: The Dynamics of Firm Lobbying
extraction.venue: NBER Working Paper 17577 (November 2011); JEL D72 D73 D78 F22 F23 J61 O31 O38
extraction.coverage: Full text read in chunks (2,394 lines, 98,889 chars): front matter, intro, data, model, estimation, immigration section, conclusion, references, all table and figure text. Appendix Table 1 and 2 lists read as headers only. Table 2 and Appendix Table 3 layout garbled, so some coefficients partly mapped. Year hint 2014 corrected to 2011 (Nov 2011 NBER WP). Paul markup: none (n_annots 0, no annot files, no p.note). Findings capped at 12; dropped access-vs-expertise point (p.19) and Nike (fn 26).
extraction.research_question: What determines the dynamics of firm lobbying over time? Do up-front entry costs explain the persistence of lobbying status, and how do firms respond to a policy shock (the 2004 expiry of the H-1B cap expansion) at the extensive versus intensive margin?
extraction.data: Unit: firm-year. (1) Compustat panel of US-headquartered publicly traded firms, 1998-2006, balanced: 3,260 firms and 29,340 observations (Table 1; regressions use 26,080 obs per Table 2 note). Lobbying from LDA semi-annual reports via Center for Responsive Politics and Senate SOPR. Industry imports from Feenstra, Romalis, Schott (UC Davis). (2) H-1B sample: 171 major firms, 2001-2006, 1,026 obs, core 846 obs (Tables 3-4). Department of Labor LCA records (1.8 million records 2001-2006); USPTO patents and inventors with ethnicity inferred from names.
extraction.method: Reduced-form linear probability model of the lobbying indicator with lagged lobbying status and up to two lagged re-entry indicators (eq 2, p.10). Table 2: Blundell-Bond GMM (cols 2-6, lag-two instruments), OLS with state, industry and year FE (col 1), within firm-FE OLS (cols 7-8, Nickell bias acknowledged). Section 5: eq 3 interacts 2001 firm dependence (log LCA count, log Chinese and Indian patenting) with a 2004-2006 binding-cap dummy, with firm and year FE, clustered by firm. Table 4: cross-section, year FE. Table 6 uses always-lobbying firms (443 obs). Table 7 tabulates by quintile.
extraction.scope: US publicly traded, US-headquartered firms in Compustat for lobbying-participation facts (1998-2006). H-1B analysis covers 171 large patenting firms present in Compustat in all of 2001-2006 and at least 0.05 percent of US domestic patents. Era of the 65,000 cap versus the 195,000 cap (1998-2004). Excludes private firms and individual lobbyists.
extraction.theory: Dynamic entry-cost model in the tradition of Roberts and Tybout (1997): a one-time sunk cost F0 to start lobbying and re-entry costs Fj after j periods without lobbying. Continuing creates an option value, so lobbying is state dependent even after controlling for profitability (Sec 3, pp.8-10). Lobbying is a legislative subsidy and signal to politicians (Deardorff and Hall 2006), per the introduction.
extraction.identification: Persistence: state dependence in lagged lobbying status identified from within-firm variation under Blundell-Bond GMM with firm effects; authors argue lagged status proxies entry costs. Policy: the 2004 expiry of the expanded H-1B cap is treated as an exogenous natural experiment, since the expiry date was fixed years earlier and the issue was not central to firms during 2001-2003 (p.13). Test is the interaction of 2001 dependence with the post-2004 dummy plus firm and year FE. Entry (extensive margin) versus adjustment (intensive margin) comparisons in Tables 5-7.
extraction.measures: Lobbying indicator = any LDA-reported lobbying in year; high-skilled immigration lobbying = specific issues naming H-1B, L-1, PERM, high-skill bills, or the phrase high-skilled immigration (pp.5-6). Lobbying expenditure from disclosure reports (mean 475k, median 164k for active firms). Firm controls: log sales, employment, assets, R&D, lagged one year; log industry imports. Dependence: log firm LCA application count 2001; log Chinese and Indian patenting 2001 (ethnicity by name-matching commercial databases, 99 percent match rate claimed). Binding cap dummy 2004-2006.
key_findings: Few firms lobby: 10 percent of 3,260 firms lobby in at least one year 1998-2006; 6.2 percent lobby in a given year (Table 1; intro p.2).
Persistence: P(lobby this year | lobbied last year) = 92 percent, above 80 percent in almost all two-digit NAICS industries (Sec 2, p.7).

Size gradient: lobbying firms average 5,407 vs 1,423 ($m) sales and 23k vs 7k employees for non-lobbying firms (Table 1); among lobbyists, correlation with spending is 28 percent for sales and 19 percent for employment (p.7).

Entry costs: lagged lobbying raises the probability of lobbying in the current year by about 88 percent in the baseline Blundell-Bond specification (text, p.10; Table 2 values 0.84-0.88 across cols 2-6). Within-FE and some other OLS values are smaller (recovered 0.44 and 0.34), but still significant per the text (p.12).
Concentration: in a typical year 96 percent of lobbying expenditure came from firms that lobbied the previous year (p.7).
Election timing: entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year; exit is unrelated to the cycle (p.7).
Policy shock: share of firms lobbying for immigration rose from 6 to 12 percent between 2003 and 2004, tracking the ratio of H-1B issuances to the cap (Fig 5, p.16).

Dependence response (Table 5): LCA-based dependence x binding cap = 0.043 (SE 0.014) for high-skill lobbying; patenting-based = 0.029 (SE 0.012). Text: 10 percent higher foreign-worker dependence raises high-skill lobbying probability by about 0.3 to 0.4 percent (p.17).

No extensive-margin response: overall any-issue lobbying coefficients near zero (-0.008 SE 0.009; -0.019 SE 0.014, column mapping inferred). Panel E of Table 7 shows 0.00 entry for the most dependent firms that had not lobbied in 2001-2003 under both measures.

Intensive margin (Table 6, 443 always-lobbying firm-years): above-median-spending firms show elasticity 0.042 (SE 0.021) LCA and 0.033 (SE 0.022) patenting; interaction terms have t-statistics under 0.5 (p.18).

Table 7 Panel D: share of most-dependent firms lobbying for high-skill immigration in 2004-2006 is 0.48 (LCA) and 0.50 (patenting) among firms that lobbied in 2001-2003, vs 0.28 and 0.27 in Panel C for 2001-2003.
Falsification: LCA and Chinese and Indian patenting show no significant link to lobbying on Clean Air and Water, Consumer Product Safety, or Retirement (pp.15-16).
limitations: Sample is publicly traded firms in Compustat; private firms unobserved; conglomerates excluded from baseline (fn 16, p.10).
Lobbying reporting threshold of 10,000 dollars per half-year; authors argue measurement error is minimal (p.6).
Dynamic GMM with T=9 relies on lag-two instruments; Arellano-Bond results more sensitive across variants (p.12).
Within FE likely biased downward (Nickell 1981); authors present the OLS results as bounds-style checks (pp.11-12).
H-1B sample is small (171 firms, 846 core obs) and selected on Compustat coverage and patenting share (p.15); core sample is 846 not the 855 maximum (fn 25).
Dependence measured only in 2001 (predetermined); LCA counts are a demand proxy; ethnicity inferred from names, not immigration status.
Authors call the evidence suggestive in Sec 5 (p.16); topic-specific spending is not disclosed, so intensity is proxied by years listed (p.19).
Abstracts from the in-house versus outside-lobbyist choice (fn 6) and from the mechanism by which lobbying raises profits (fn 14).
Cap expiry assumed exogenous, though firms knew of it years in advance (p.13).
short_quotes: The probability that a firm lobbies in the current year given that it lobbied in the previous year is 92%.
These results support the existence of significant barriers to entry in the lobbying process.
All of the adjustments among these major patenting firms in response to the policy change were intensive margin adjustments.
references_of_note: Roberts and Tybout (1997), American Economic Review 87: sunk-cost entry model that the lobbying model follows.
Bombardini (2008), J Int Econ 75: firm heterogeneity and lobby participation with up-front costs.
Grossman and Helpman (2001), Special Interest Politics: fixed costs of lobbying.
Blundell and Bond (1998), J Econometrics 87: GMM estimator used in baseline.
Facchini, Mayda, Mishra (2011), J Int Econ 85: interest groups and US immigration policy.
Kerr and Lincoln (2010), J Labor Econ 28: H-1B reforms and ethnic invention, source of dependence measures.
Bertrand, Bombardini, Trebbi (2011): whom you know versus what you know in lobbying (access vs expertise).

summary_md: Kerr, Lincoln and Mishra (NBER WP 17577, Nov 2011; the AEJ: Economic Policy version is dated 2014) study why firm lobbying is so persistent. In a balanced Compustat panel of 3,260 US-headquartered public firms, 1998-2006, only 10 percent lobby in any year and 6.2 percent in a given year. Among firms that lobbied last year, 92 percent lobby again. In a typical year, 96 percent of lobbying dollars come from firms that lobbied the year before. The authors read this as evidence of sunk entry costs in a Roberts-Tybout model. A Blundell-Bond linear probability model puts the lagged-status effect at about 0.84-0.88. Within-firm fixed-effects OLS gives about 0.44, which the authors say is biased downward (Nickell). Entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year itself, and exit does not follow the cycle. The policy test uses the 2004 lapse of the expanded H-1B cap. They interact each firm's 2001 dependence on foreign workers with a 2004-2006 dummy, with firm and year fixed effects, in 171 large patenting firms (846 core firm-years). Dependence raises lobbying on high-skill immigration (0.043, SE 0.014, LCA measure). It does not raise the chance of lobbying at all (-0.008, SE 0.009). No highly dependent non-lobbyist entered. All of the response came from firms that were already lobbying (the intensive margin). For Paul's systems this is mainly evidence about forecasting and specification. It backs Mentat's persistence-anchored lobbying forecasts, which leave out election-phase effects. It warns about the lagged-outcome lobbying equation with sector fixed effects in the sector growth study. It also shows that LDA reports cannot measure spending per issue, which is what the contested-bills question would need. The firm-level, 1998-2006 public-firm scope limits how far any of this transfers.

bearings.paper_claim: Participation persistence: P(lobby this year given lobbied last year) = 92 percent in a balanced 3,260-firm Compustat panel, 1998-2006 (6.2 percent lobby in a given year; 10.0 percent ever lobby). Above 80 percent in almost all two-digit NAICS industries. 96 percent of expenditures in a typical year come from prior-year lobbyists. Entry clusters in the year before an election, not the election year; exit is unrelated to the cycle.

summary_issues: Summary asserts the AEJ Economic Policy version is dated 2014. The analyst text is the NBER WP 17577 of November 2011 and the AEJ version is not in the file; unverified here.
Summary says dependence does not raise the chance of lobbying at all (-0.008, SE 0.009). That is a negative insignificant LCA any-issue estimate (Table 5 column 3); say no detectable effect.

Summary says the paper backs Mentat persistence-anchored lobbying forecasts. Evidence is on firm participation, not sector dollars; say it is consistent with the design, with the transfer caveat.
Summary says LDA reports cannot measure spending per issue. The paper says only that amounts per specific topic are not required (p.19); reports do list totals.

paul_alignment (not summary): Paul's cycle-model note says lobbying peaks in election years, and Paul holds that returns motivate deep pockets. Item has no Paul annotations (paul_entries empty); neither statement was found in the refit README or the brain topic files checked.

gaps_exposed: No extensive-margin view: sector totals over a fixed roster of companies cannot separate entry and exit from changes in incumbent spending. Kerr shows the two behave differently, and crypto and fintech entry would show up only as level jumps.

The lobbying equation in the sector study's original contract (lagged outcome plus sector FE) has no stated treatment of Nickell bias. The implemented core drops the lag entirely, and neither choice is documented against the dynamic-panel problem.

No literature backs the 2026-10-01 ruling that exempts lobbying from the election-phase adjustment. Kerr's pre-election-year entry result is a testable reason, but the odd-year entry effect is not measured in Mentat.
The contested-bills question about relative spend has no measurement, because LDA does not disclose spend per issue or per bill.

melange-lobbying.fec-lda-bridge: Kerr shows lagged lobbying status and firm size absorb most of the variation in participation. Any later bridge design would need to condition on both. The current product rule bars FEC as a lobbying predictor, so this is noted, not proposed.
flags: Year mismatch: the text file is NBER WP 17577 (Nov 2011). The slug and the year hint of 2014 refer to the AEJ: Economic Policy version, and coefficients may differ from the published tables.

Mentat never adds the two, and the sector config notes that undifferentiated sums double count self-filers' outside fees. Do not compare the magnitudes directly.
The Nickell-bias reading of the sector-study lobbying equation is new agent analysis and is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
No conflict with the barred SNA proposals or with D-025. The paper uses LDA for firm identity and participation, not edges, which is consistent with D-021.
paul_alignment: No annotations on this work. It is cited in the sector growth study, where Paul holds that returns motivate deep pockets. Kerr partly agrees: size predicts who lobbies. But here yearly changes follow persistence and issue shocks, which fits the null growth result better than a confident ROI reading. Paul's cycle-model note says lobbying syncs with elections and peaks in election years. Kerr qualifies that: entry peaks the year before and exit is acyclical. The built system already exempts lobbying from the phase adjustment (README:152), so his note is stale.
